utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Today we'll be sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis with Judge Morrison being away due to his urgent personal matters. Before we continue to hear the evidence, the Chamber will issue an oral ruling on the Prosecution's motion to exclude the evidence of witness Goran Sikiras filed on the 26th of November, 2012, wherein the Prosecution seeks the execution or, in the alternative, the partial exclusion of Goran Sikiras's evidence on the basis that it is for the most part irrelevant as it pertains to crimes committed against Serbs and that the remainder of the proposed evidence is duplicative of evidence already admitted and/or of low probative value. The accused filed his response on the 27th of November, 2012, opposing the motion and arguing that Sikiras's evidence is relevant to events in the municipality of Vogosca in 1992. More particularly, he submits that the evidence shows that Bosnian Serbs did not make unprovoked attacks in Vogosca and that: "These expulsions and killings were not the result of a joint criminal enterprise to expel or kill Muslims but were part of a civil war in which each side attacked the other." The Chamber notes that about half of Sikiras's statement is concerned with crimes committed against Bosnian Serbs in Vogosca and as such are not relevant to the charges in the indictment. I refer here to page 4, parts of page 5, as well as pages 6 and 7. The Chamber reminds the accused once again that it will not admit detailed tu quoque evidence under the guise of relevance to this trial. However, the Chamber considers that the remainder of Sikiras's statement is of some relevance to the background to the take-over of Vogosca. And the Chamber therefore grants the motion in part and excludes page 4, starting from line 2; page 5, except the three paragraphs starting with, first, on the 5th of May, 1992; second, on the 12th of May, 1992; and finally on the 8th of June 1992; page 6 in its entirety; and page 7 in its entirety except the witness's acknowledgement as well as the associated exhibits referred therein. The Chamber allows the remainder of Goran Sikiras's statement to be tendered pursuant to Rule 92 ter should the accused still wish to call him to testify in this trial. In light of the redactions made to the statement, the Chamber orders that the Prosecution shall have 30 minutes for its cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, may I say something not necessarily related to this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has nothing to do with this decision but the way I understand the indictment and what I stand accused of. I am accused of having ordered all of those events as if I had caused fear amongst the Serbs and that everything was fine before the SDS and Karadzic came along setting a chain of events in motion. It is my understanding of the indictment is that many events generated themselves, not by the tu quoque principle but simply by virtue of orders of local commanders or that things were dictated by the events themselves. That is why it is relevant to see what one side had gone through and the other as well before all that. One needs to understand the behaviour and mentality of the three ethnic communities and it goes beyond the mere orders. This is the broader concept which stands against the idea of a joint criminal enterprise. This was a civil war which was the umpteenth civil war that these ethnicities engaged in and it was not part of a JCE but a result of history and having these three ethnicities kill each other through centuries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll stop you. That does not necessarily mean that you have to allude to the evidence of crimes against you for each and every -- for each and every witness. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll leave it at that at the moment. Let's bring in the witness, unless there's any other matters to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we're bringing in the witness this isn't something that needs to be done out of his presence but during his direct examination we would be wanting to use a video that was disclosed to us yesterday by the Prosecution and we would like to have permission to add that to our 65 ter list, since it wasn't in our possession at the time it was created.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Your request is granted, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, and good morning to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need to intervene in the transcript. Line 1, page 3, I said the following, [In English] "... simply by orders of local commanders." [Interpretation] I said the following: Were the events ordered by local commanders or were they caused by some preceding similar events: [In English] "But simply by orders of local commanders and that things were dictated by the events themselves." So it is contrary. Not by order of local commanders but by other events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, before Dr. Karadzic begins, I note again and as I said, I don't feel it's for the Prosecution to ask for this because this is not our witness, but in the interests of the witness, I would suggest -- in the interest of the witness and so he's aware of his rights, I would suggest he be given advice pursuant to Rule 90(E), and I just thought it would be better to do that before we go any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I think that in this instance you should not give any warning. The Prosecution should ask for such a warning before it's -- the testimony of the witness commences. When you give it a warning in the middle of the witness's testimony or before they start the cross-examination, it adds an emphasis to -- to it as if the witness has some reason to worry about what his answers are going to be and what his own rights are in these proceedings, and we think it's -- it's always out of an abundance of caution to give someone a warning before they start their testimony and if the Prosecution thinks it's appropriate, that's the time to do it, but if they don't do it then, as far as we're concerned, it's waived and it shouldn't be given in the middle of a witness's testimony. And this isn't the first time that that has happened so I think you should set a hard and fast rule that if the Prosecution believes such a warning is appropriate, they should ask for it before the witness commences his testimony, and if they don't no warning will be given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I find it a bit difficult to follow your submission, Mr. Robinson. If warning is warranted, it should be given whether or not it is belated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think it's intimidating to a witness to give him a warning in the middle of his testimony about what

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Is a warning by the Chamber something threatening the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think it indicates that the witness may have reason to have concern. You don't give this to every witness. You only give it to witnesses who you're being asked or told to have some reason to fear self-incrimination. So when you do that in the middle of a witness's testimony then you're sending a message to the witness that he has some reason to fear from the answers that he gives, and we think that ought to be done very cautiously.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And all this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- is being done in the presence of the witness who seems -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to stop you, because the French translation was still going on. Did you finish your submission, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I didn't anticipate Mr. Robinson's submission, but if this is going to go further, perhaps the witness should be asked whether he understand English or to remove his headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic, I heard you saying thank you or good morning in English, but do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A couple of words, but in principle, I don't understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you kindly take off your headphone for some time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, assuming the Chamber were to assure the witness that he has nothing to -- he hasn't -- he doesn't have to feel intimidated in any way by this morning, would that be able to cure the situation of the late warning, would you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I think that would be a good idea. But it would also be good to set a rule in the future so that it doesn't happen again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I concerning the differences in language. Today Madam Edgerton has kindly offered a better expression, to be advised rather than to be warned, and I thank her for that, Madam Edgerton. And also I would like if the obliged term, "obliged," which is expressed by the Chamber not to be translated "the Chamber has the right to force you," but rather "to oblige you."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: That is the term -- interpreter's note: That is the term which is used in the official translation of the Rules. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the future, Mr. Tieger and Ms. Edgerton, I would like you to bring that issue before witnesses take the stand and give solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So Gospodin Mijatovic, you can wear your head phone again. We should have done that yesterday, but before you continue to give evidence, I would like to draw your attention to a particular Rule here at the Tribunal. Under this Rule, Rule 90(E), you may object to answering a question from the Prosecution or the accused or from the Judges if you believe that your answer will incriminate you. When I say "incriminate," I mean that something you say may amount to an admission of your guilt for a criminal offence or could provide evidence that you have committed an offence. However, even if you think your answer will incriminate you and you do not wish to answer the question, the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question, but in such a case the Tribunal will make sure that your testimony compelled in such a way shall not be used as evidence in other case against you for any offence other than false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] More or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic, I just want to add just a bit to what the President has said. You must not in any way feel intimidated by what the President has just told you. What he has done is to apprise you of your rights as laid down by the Rules. So don't in any way feel intimidated or fearful. This is very important. Do you understand this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Judge Baird.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Major Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 1D6291 in e-court. Translation is pending with this one as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You authored this document. Do you recall this document? Are you able to identify it? It is your report to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall it. It is my document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it say the following, "At 8.30 and 11.00 p.m.," and in the second paragraph "at 11.10 there were certain things taking place. Were you always this precise when keeping track of events?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you focus on the second paragraph and read it, please. There is the mention of a sniper.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A sniper from Stojcevacki Siljak from the direction of Polje on Nedzarici where at 11.10 he was wounded in his arm -- or the following were wounded in their arm: A Govedarica born in 1973 and a shot arrived from the area called government receipts a born in 1973 and a shot arrived from the area called Pancirka where UNPROFOR is deployed. We did not return fire except when engaging the Pancirka building and we did not sustain any casualties. We have one wounded fighter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So who was it who fired from the Pancirka building where UNPROFOR was?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we presumed it was the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it something unusual that they opened fire in close proximity of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was nothing out of the ordinary. It was standard practice. They fired from positions in the vicinity of UNPROFOR. They had 105-millimetre guns across the building from the PTT Inzinjering where the UNPROFOR headquarters were. They also had positions in underground parking lots in Alipasino Polje, and from there they would pull out guns and opened fire on the Serb Ilidza, Rajlovac, and Lukavica. When we returned fire, UNPROFOR protested to our side why we were engaging areas in their proximity. When they protested, we asked them, Why do you allow them to be anywhere near you? We have to respond to their fire. We cannot allow our children and civilians to be killed in Ilidza, because that kind of shelling usually was targeting Ilidza where the school and hospital were as well as outpatient clinics and health centres. Both health centres in Ilidza were destroyed as a result of such shelling. This was nothing extraordinary. Quite to the contrary, this was routinely happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Major.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document marked for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D6291 becomes Exhibit D2511, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To be marked for identification, yes. Yes, continue. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 1D8566 next. I believe this one has a translation. I kindly ask for it not to be broadcast, because there is a name mentioned in the document, your Excellencies, so as not to be in breach of your tu quoque decision. We won't tender this document because it contains information of rapes of Serb women. Rather, we will ask the major to read out a sentence for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Major, is it correct that this man, the Muslim fighter whose name is mentioned in the document, was in contact with you and finally defected to the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we look at the end of paragraph 3, but do not mention his name.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That person, between November of 1992 and December 1993, as a fighter of the so-called Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, used a hand-held mortar and an automatic rifle in the theatre of war around Sarajevo having killed 13 soldiers of the VRS and a guard at Elektroprivreda and Bristol. He also killed two Serb civilians across the Miljacka River.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is this Bristol?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a hotel, the Bristol Hotel in Novo Sarajevo, facing Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the portion read out for the transcript suffices, I seek to tender it. Otherwise, it is up to you to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see the need on your part to tender it as you indicated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I would like to show four brief video-clips from --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Five, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That I received late last night. Some of them we haven't had the time to translate, and for the three of these video-clips we have received translation from the Prosecution, but for the other two we haven't. So I would appreciate being -- if we could show 1D468 -- 6480. Could we play this video-clip from 2 minutes 14 seconds; from the beginning up until 2 minutes and 14 seconds. And I believe that's the longest video-clip.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the exact reference of where this video-clip is in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you play, Mr. Karadzic, I just received a note from the interpreters that they do not have the exact reference.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, for the first two we haven't received the translation, and we haven't managed to provide it ourselves. That's for the first two. And for the other three, we have them. So I would appreciate the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, in cases where we do not have the transcription, we know that we have difficulty hearing the translations. So why don't we start with those portions with transcript. Let's see how we can get on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In that case could we have 6482, please. From 7 minutes 13 seconds up until 8 minutes and 42 seconds. 7.13.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Europe is becoming more aware of the fact that the real threat to its democracy, justice and freedom is coming from the jihad which has been waged in this region for four years now with its main protagonists being real war criminals and bloodthirsty beasts like Izetbegovic, Ganic, Silajdzic, Delic, who have emerged from a fundamentalist marriage, imposing unseen terror causing more than 15.000 Serbs to become victims only in the part of Sarajevo that is under Turkish converts. They have lived through horrific atrocities originating from the clouded minds of Juka Prazina, Bajramovic, Delic, Dedic, and other fundamentalist criminals, all upon orders of the monsters most responsible from the former Bosnia and Herzegovina. To this day, screams can be heard in their prisons, especially in the notorious Tarcin concentration camp and a number of prisons in Sarajevo, Tuzla, Konjic, Visoko, and Zenica, all the while they have their mouths full of lies about multi-ethnic, multi-religious Bosnia and the democratic order of their Bosnia." Interpreter's note: The last portion was missing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This suffices.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Major, sir, where did you get this bit of information that over 15.000 Serbs were victims in Sarajevo, and does this mean that they were killed or were they victims in other ways too?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information that we had at our disposal came from witness statements, witnesses who fled Sarajevo and crossed over to our territory, and this is information that intelligence services, both military and civilian, gathered on the ground. And, Mr. President, this will later be confirmed as true, but if you would like me to give a full answer to your question, I would have to elaborate a bit. Well, first what I said is that it became clear to everyone, and up until now there was a deliberate cover-up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic, I think you have answered the question. I'm struggling to understand the relevance of this part to your case. It may relate to the credibility. Please continue, yes. We'll see. We'll find -- we'll find out at the end of this part of the answer. We'll deal with the admission. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm really sorry, Your Honour, but we have no LiveNote on this side of the courtroom, any of us. I don't know if anybody else is similarly affected or afflicted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see any problem from the Bench. Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ours is working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it the Registrar will arrange something for you, Ms. Edgerton. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then I won't ask you where you got the information that Prazina, Bajramovic, Celo and others were criminals, but let me just ask this: What you stated at this rally and what was happening there, what kind of impact did this have on the morale among the civilians and military on Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it certainly had an impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What kind of impact? What were the effects?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, people understood, and this was just another confirmation, that their superhuman fight, struggle, in Serbian Ilidza was justified. Mr. President, when I say superhuman struggle let me explain it this way: The Serbian Ilidza and the people who attended this rally fought the entire war with an enemy that was six times stronger than it was. The Serb Ilidza had the largest number of casualties or killed people in -- of all other Serbian municipalities. It had 932 killed people, about 500 dead civilians, and the effect was -- and the reason was -- the consequences was that the Ilidza Brigade had four brigades on other side. The enemy had four brigades, the 104th, 105th, 102nd and 104th [as interpreted]. And let me just give you some information on one of these brigades. The 104th Brigade had five heavy armoured personnel carriers. It had five combat vehicles. It had five 152-howitzers. It had five 105-millimetre howitzer. It had ten recoilless guns. All the fighters had automatic weapons. In other words, the Serbian Ilidza suffered the biggest losses of all municipalities, both among the ranks and among civilians. And as a result, although people knew throughout the war what the enemy had as its intention, their intention was to cut through Serbian Ilidza and link up with the Muslim forces in Central Bosnia, which would then make our position far heavier, because there would be a hundred thousand so-called members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina who then be operational and could be active throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina and to be far deadlier and engage all the front lines where the Serbian people and the Serbian fighters were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 1D6483, please. From 8 minutes 44 to 9 minutes 07.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Today the entire world knows that when Alija Izetbegovic was trying to justify to his associates the reasons why he had ordered the massacre against his people in the Vase Miskina Street and Markale I and II, he responded that the Koran had obliged them to do it, that no price was too high when it came to the Islamic goal."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in relation to this, the incidents that you mentioned, that you said were caused by the Muslim side, did the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps investigate whether this was committed by someone on the Serb side and what basis did you have for this claim that this was actually perpetrated by them?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the base for my claim is very specific, Mr. President. I was fortunate to come by information, and because I hadn't had much time, I didn't have a chance to present them to the Defence, but I will tell you about it now so that you can see what I'm talking about. One day military police came to the command and reported that there was a man who had crossed over from Sarajevo to our side and who wanted to talk to me. I asked him what his name was, and he said -- may I mention his name, first and last, or do we have to move to private session for his security, for his safety?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, better skip his name, if you can. But if necessary, we can ask to have -- to get the name from you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is this video-clip, and it was broadcast on the Radio Television of Republika Srpska during the war. This man was the son of a late friend of mine. This late friend of mine was, I believe, a Croat, but believe me, I'm not really sure, because we never asked who was of what ethnicity. We were -- although we worked for 15 years, I had no idea, and I'm not even sure to this day. And the name -- his first and last name frequently appears both in the Serbian and the Croatian people. So I never asked him what ethnicity he was. All I wanted -- all I cared about was that someone was a good human being. Now, his mother was Muslim. I knew that. And when late Pero died - and I can use this name because it's very frequent - at the time I was one of the directors in Feroelektro and I would go and speak at funerals, and as you recall, there were both religious rites and civilian rites, and what we would do at funerals, we would go and ask them what type of rites they wanted. So anyway, I went and -- to this funeral and spoke there, and this young man, he remembered that. So he risked his life later on, went through a minefield and came to see me, and he said to me, Well, you know, I remember you very well from the funeral. My father said you were a good man. You spoke so well. So I came to talk to you. Now, I knew that he had come from a very difficult place, that there were a lot of people of different ethnicity there, that it was very difficult to survive, and he risked his life, came through the minefield. And I asked him what I could do for him, and he said, Well, I would like to go to Belgrade. I have a friend there. And if I don't manage to get a job there, I would like to move on from there to one of the European countries. So if you could help me with this. Now, to make you understand what the atmosphere was, I offered him coffee and something to eat at the time, and I told him --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic, could you slow down in your speaking. And put a pause, Mr. Karadzic. I'm not sure the interpretation has been concluded. We had the interpretation until the part where you said: "Now, to make you understand what the atmosphere was, I offered him coffee and something to eat at the time ..." Is that all that you said, or did you say --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I offered him coffee and food. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what was the content of the information that you received?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he told me -- well, I asked him, What did you do all this time there? As far as I can recall, it would have been two years that had passed since the beginning of the war, so approximately it was at that time. So I asked him, What have you done all this time and how did you manage? And he said, Well, I am an audio technician, and I worked on -- at Radio Sarajevo, and on the day of the diversion at Vase Miskina Street when we arrived at work sometime before 7.00, we were sent to the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not get the location.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vecna Vatra. Now, that is close to Vase Miskina Street. He said I went there with a colleague of mine, a journalist, and we waited there. It was rather cold. We were rather nervous, and we agreed that I should go because the electroshop was there and I recall even now that the manager of that shop was Avdo. Now I asked him if I could use his phone to call from there because there were no mobile phones at the time, so I called from that shop and I called the editor of the radio station and asked him, How long are we supposed to stay here and what are we waiting for, because there is no rally, there's nothing going on, there is no one showing up, so what are we doing here? We are just freezing. And this man answered to him, Well, just stay there. It will happen very soon, and so don't protest too much. And if you protest, there are lines for people like you. Now let me explain what lines are, that's front lines where the fighting was. I went up to my friend at Vecna Vatra and told him what the answer of the editor was and at that point in time we heard the blast, the sound of the blast and then we realised so this was our task that's why we were there. We were supposed to be there on site so that we could report immediately on what was going on, the suffering and the screams of the people on the bread line. So this is what we learned about Vase Miskina Street that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps after these incidents or, rather, do you know whether they had investigated this in order to establish whether it was perpetrated by the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. And because of this propaganda of the enemy side where they would always blame all the suffering on the Serbs both their leadership and the public officials, they would always accuse the Serb side of these things and blame it on the Serb side. And so in order to make sure and be absolutely certain of what was happening you had to conduct an investigation. So that's why it was conducted. And there was absolutely no doubt whatsoever that it hadn't been done by the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the third video-clip now. That's 6484 from 9 minutes 18 to 9 minutes 45.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] For this brief period of time and it was November 1995 when honourable and courageous journalists finally decided to visit Serb Sarajevo. They saw our mothers in mourning, our cemeteries, our destroyed and burned homes, our crippled children, realising how shamelessly manipulated they had been up to then by Turkish converts and their media."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what this means that it was only in November that journalists started coming to see you to find out the truth?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, the truth about the suffering of the Serb people, Mr. President, had a very difficult path to traverse as is the case today, Mr. President. What happened to the Serb people, these crimes committed against us, preparations were carried out a lot before that, before 1992. I'm just going to tell this distinguished Court and this distinguished gathering. It is indispensable for me to say the following as far as suffering is concerned: Gentlemen, the brigade that I commanded, over those four years lost over 460 fighters; 2.150 were wounded in my brigade, which is highly characteristic. Judge, please, may I just finish. I'm finishing right now. I'm saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you try to answer the question. The question was not about the sufferings themselves but why it was only in November that journalists started coming to see you to find out the truth. Could you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've already said that these people who had intended for the Serb people to suffer and to be destroyed, well, there's a very strong link there because they were on orders to by-pass us and therefore the truth could not reach the rest of the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These journalists and crews that were in Sarajevo, CNN, BBC, et cetera, did they go to Ilidza? Did they cross over? Did they go to check the information they received?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, rather, one would have to say no, although there were exceptions, truth to tell, but then they would also distort things. When they'd get in contact with us, they would try to persuade us that they had sent accurate reports as to what was happening on the ground and that it was only in their newspaper and TV offices that the news were further distorted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 6480, please. Could we please have that now, these two clips that do not have a translation. Two minutes and half a minute. They are highly important for us and relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any objection, Ms. Edgerton, or observation?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't quite know what to say, Your Honours. This is something he only received last evening, after all. I'm sorry I can't offer anything further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's see. Let us see how we got on with it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the beginning, so 6480, 1D6480 from the beginning until 2:14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, there's no point. We don't get any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I kindly ask the booth to interpret as they interpret simultaneously when we are speaking.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It is too fast for simultaneous interpretation and we have not been provided with a transcript of what is being said in the original either, let alone the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your legal advisors heard the interpretation. Consult with them how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, is it possible to play a small portion of the recording, stop it and then continue it so that the interpretation can be effected?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we pause here and let's deal with the three portions we've heard so far, then that may shed a light how to proceed. I take it you are tendering those three portions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And can I hear from you, Ms. Edgerton, about those three portions we have heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No objection to the three portions, Your Honour, and in fact, I propose to use further portion during the cross-examination. So it may be a matter that Your Honours -- where Your Honours might want to deal with the whole video that these are drawn from at the end of things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber has some difficulty in -- in relation to certain parts of the -- the portions, in particular with respect to their relevance, but if you are going to use some part of it for whatever use -- I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We deal with the admissibility of these portions at the end of this witness's evidence. I have to ask interpreters whether the suggestion made by the Defence is feasible.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We believe not. It is too fast, and it would require consecutive interpretation, which is quite different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think the thing to do would be to try to take it -- make a transcript of this over the weekend and play this portion with the witness on Monday if -- if it's important enough for Dr. Karadzic to believe it's important enough to make the witness stay, I think that's the best solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can he not elicit evidence from the witness without having to rely on this video?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, could we do this? I mean it's not very long. It's two and a half minutes, 2 minutes, 40 seconds. Could we play it for the witness and then put questions to him and we are going to deal with admissibility and the translation later. So it would be for the witness to know what he is affirming or denying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, if we the Chamber or the -- if the Chamber nor the Prosecution is not able to follow what he said in this transcript what's the point of playing this at all?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, that's what I was about to say. I don't know at all what's in the non-transcribed versions, and it's really just another way of leading the witness. So it would seem to me if Dr. Karadzic has information from this that he wishes to -- or based on this that he wishes to adduce to the witness he can put that to the witness and have him affirm it now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm sorry that I have to say this, that we received this exhibit that was there to begin with, if we had received it on time, we would have translated all of it as the OTP had translated everything that they were interested in. Fifteen minutes -- 15 minutes was enough to have all of that translated. I'm not criticising Madam Edgerton. It was somebody else who omitted to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you find it very important, I heard the French booth translated a bit, so we can repeat how many minutes it may take. Let's try it. It's your time. It's up to you how to use your time. So we'll try -- we can play many times and that's with the indulgence of the translators. We can give it a try. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just to make -- to be perfectly clear, this was not there, nor was it in our possession, and we went actually to some pretty extraordinary efforts to get this to the Defence counsel as soon -- as soon as we received it, and that was -- and were able to have access to the video and that was last evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll play first so the interpreters could hear the general context and try again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: That cannot be a full accurate interpretation of the entire video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It should be -- we understand. Let's play it first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How long do we need? Do you need all these portions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first one is only 2:14, and the other one is 30 seconds, and the first one is 2 minutes, 14 seconds, or, actually, can we stop here and then I can put questions to the major.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We didn't hear the interpretation. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, that's kind of the thing. We didn't hear any interpretation, and I know my colleagues are very professional in this and do their best, and to keep playing this like this is really almost kind of effectively leading the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think what we have here are the witness's words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Let us stop here, and if necessary, you call the witness again next week -- be it next week or a month away. I think that's the most efficient way at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I just put a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that 800 shells fell in the civilian zone and that six women were wounded?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Leading. Leading question, Mr. Karadzic. But could you ask when he interviewed this and when he made this speech, on what occasion or -- those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That speech, those first three that we played, when was that held and under what conditions?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, this speech was made at a rally after Dayton, after the Dayton agreement. That is to say after the 21st of November, 1995, in Luzani. I think that that would be an answer to your question, a specific answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This settlement was defended, but you had to leave it after Dayton?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was defended like ten other municipalities of the Serb Sarajevo, but we had to leave it, unfortunately, on the basis of the decision reached in Dayton, all of these settlements and all of this, also all of western Ilidza that we defended with our own blood. And I think it would only be proper for me to speak about this in memory of these people, the Serb municipality of Ilidza sustained the greatest losses in that previous war in -- out of all of Republika Srpska I think that if you look at all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Ilidza had the highest number of losses including military losses and civilians losses. Please do not doubt this. Thirty-five mortars only, and also I mentioned the howitzers and other weapons a moment ago. One of the brigades opposite us, the 104th, had that, the one attacking from Sokolovic Kolonija, Butmir and Hrasnica. So they had 70 artillery pieces and weapons. This is 50 shells. That's already 700 shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. I'm sorry about these two video-clips. Probably we are going to call again when we have the translation. I just wanted to ask you about the shelling of the waterworks -- or, rather, electricity facilities. However, we'll do that when we receive the translation. We'll do it later. Thank you. We have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Has this been admitted, these three, these three where we had this translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I told you we would deal with it after his evidence is over in its entirety, after seeing the portion the Prosecution is going to use, if any.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What time do Your Honours anticipate the first break this morning?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just in relation to the evidence that you gave to Dr. Karadzic during your examination-in-chief, I wonder if you could tell us actually the name of the military policeman who crossed to your side from Sarajevo and gave you the information about the bread line shelling that you recounted?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that. That is a misinterpretation, very poor interpretation. On the contrary, he was an audio technician in

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, also in your statement, you referred actually to receiving information from, among other things, commanding officers of the BiH Army who collaborated with you. Who were they? What were their names?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to tell you this: I think that your question is misplaced. Tell me anyone in the world who would tell on someone who had provided him with information so that the next day that person could get killed?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If -- if it may assist, perhaps the witness could say this in closed session so that it remains under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, Mr. President. No one ever says anything like that. And ultimately when I said "we," that means -- I mean, look, this information -- I mean, let me respond to Madam Prosecutor. You probably know this even without me telling you, but let me remind you: There was always a two-way street as far as information was concerned, communication between the headquarters and the brigades and thereby battalions as well. Do you understand what I'm saying? So in the battalion we gathered certain information, then they sent it to us at the brigade commands and then we forwarded that information to the corps command and then that is only logical in any army of the world. So that means that -- I mean, when we had this information that was coming from up and down, in this information our superiors had these people who collaborated with them, because that confirm -- that was confirmed to me several times. An attack would sort of take place at such and such a place. So it is not that this was this well-known sorceress that was trying to foretell what would happen. It was based on intelligence. It was -- yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Pausing there, could we move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mijatovic, today in the transcript you talked and made some mention about weapons held by the forces of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina that were facing you, and I just want to ask you on the other side because you haven't mentioned it to confirm some of the weapons held by your brigade, the Ilidza Brigade. Can you confirm that your brigade had three T-55 tanks?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you confirm that your brigade, at least in 1993, had a total of 30 sniper rifles?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we did not have a single one, at least I wasn't aware of any, and I can only tell you what I know. Why do I say that? We didn't need sniper rifles, Madam Prosecutor. The separation lines were de facto useless. The demarcation line was on Ilidza, and we were only separated by a street, that is to say the width of 10 to 12 metres. Anyone knows that in such a situation a sniper rifle is less reliable than a simple sidearm that you can use to shoot at someone across the street.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Maybe we could, given your answer, have a look at a document, 65 ter 23830. It's -- and while that's being called up, could I just ask you to confirm that Vladimir Radojcic was one of the commanders of the Ilidza Brigade? Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see a document, but there's no signature by the colonel -- or lieutenant-colonel, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm really very sorry, but it seems like now I've completely lost -- or we've completely lost any ability to see the documents in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could we change from Sanction to e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The booths cannot see it either. Now we can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You see the document on the screen in front of you, and it has the name Vladimir Radojcic at the bottom. Vladimir Radojcic in 1993, 1994, and 1995 --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- was the Ilidza Brigade commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now this document dated 29 October 1993 responds to something from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command reporting that the brigade has a total of 30 sniper rifles, M-76 and M-48, one silencer and one passive infrared device. So, actually, your knowledge as to what the brigade had in terms of sniper rifles seems to be incorrect.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see what it says here. Let me tell you this: On the 31st of October, I wasn't in the brigade that day, and I was in no position to see anything. Why? Because as it happened, the 31st of October is the holiday of Saint Lucas, which is the patron saint of my family and mine. If there were any possibilities for that, we did our best to be at home that day, to be with our family. The same goes for Christmas and the most important holidays. The 31st of October is the day when I was definitely not in a position to see this document. That is why I told you that I am personally unaware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But then you don't dispute that -- the accuracy of this document, do you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot deny this. I am in no position to either confirm or deny.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could that be a Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's okay, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number would be P6014, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's about time to take a break, but given that we'll be concluding a bit earlier than usual, I'm asking the parties about taking just half an hour break for today.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's completely fine with me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'd like that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: That is fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it that's fine with the court reporter. Thank you. We'll have a break for 30 minutes and resume at 5 past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I was wondering if I might raise a very small scheduling issue very quickly, or I can do it at the end of the session, as the Court wishes. I just wanted to note that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's do that at the end of the session. And as regards the debate we had in private session, I was of the opinion that we can lift the confidentiality of the transcript from line 3 on page 31, but if the parties have a different opinion, please let me know before the end of today's session. Yes, Ms. Edgerton. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mijatovic, we were on the subject of weapons held by your brigade, and we just finished talking about sniper rifles. Do you also agree that your brigade had howitzers in its possession?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 105 and 155 millimetre?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for 155s, I don't think we had any, but we definitely did have 105s.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpret's note: Could the witness approach the microphone. We cannot hear him.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic, the interpreters have asked if you could just slide in a little more so you're closer to the microphone so the interpreters can hear you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And 120-millimetre mortars?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 76-millimetre guns?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's just talk quickly about the numbers of each. How many howitzers?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know there were two as far as I recall. We had two 105s; we had one ZiS, the recoilless gun; we had three tanks; three APCs; we had several pieces of 122-millimetre [as interpreted] mortars and 62-millimetre mortars and 82-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How many is several? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely more than two 110-millimetre pieces [as interpreted]. Well, I'm not sure about the rest. I'm trying to recall. I didn't think about that much. As for 82-millimetre pieces, we had at least seven or eight. 60-millimetre pieces there were four or five. The number of armoured vehicles, I believe I have shared that with you already. One ZiS, which is 186-millimetre [as interpreted] gun. We had one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that some of the figures in the transcript are wrong. It is not "186" but "76," and the mortar is "120" rather than "122." The 122 piece is a different artillery piece. Perhaps that can be clarified later in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Mijatovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. I've never heard of 176-millimetre calibre. The ZiS, as it was called, was an old -- which was an old kind of weapon was called Jarac [phoen] in the previous war.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 11, "110 millimetres," several pieces, whereas it should have been mortar 120 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no calibre 110. There is only the 100 and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down when citing figures.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no 110. I can see it on the screen as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your evidence today you talked about how Bosnian forces fired from UNPROFOR and pulled out guns from underground parking lots in Alipasino Polje and you returned fire. Now, you lived in Alipasino Polje yourself for a period of time; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you would agree with me that it's a densely populated residential area with low and very high-rise apartment buildings; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Alipasino Polje mainly had high-rise buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Where civilians lived; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you marked in one of the associated exhibits with your statement a map with military targets, D2499, and those were all in and around the area where you used to live, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So your evidence is that you fired at these objects that are listed in paragraph 9, which are found within densely populated residential area.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As it was interpreted to me, we fired at objects. When you say an object in our language, one usually pictures a family house or an apartment building. We never fired at such buildings where civilians lived, because we had our orders, strict orders that we abided by. We also abided by the international laws of war and the Geneva Conventions. We never opened fire like that. I don't know if you --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said objects.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never fired at objects where civilians lived.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My question was related to the military targets you listed in paragraph 9, and my question was you fired at these objects which you had just agreed were in a residential area; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We only engaged combat targets. We never engaged apartment buildings or areas where there were civilians. That is out of the question. So my answer was very clear. We only engaged targets from where fire was opened against us. So we engaged targets that targeted us, that killed us, only those targets on the other side, fire targets, combat targets from which fire was opened on us.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And those are legitimate targets, you have to admit.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about this a little bit more. These targets were in areas where civilians lived. So it's reasonable to expect civilians to be in the immediate area of these targets; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is even more reasonable to expect a warring party, in other words, the enemy side, not to open fire from civilian areas, because that other side, the opposing side, will open fire on our targets and then they expect that we would return fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you did.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your -- we only engaged combat targets. In other words, we returned fire. We only returned fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fire on --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the previous reply, it did not make into the transcript the words of the witness who said that they sowed death amongst our ranks, and this is not something that made it into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Mijatovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What the President said, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And as you have noted, if you speak so fast, your words will be -- some part of your answer will -- will miss the interpretation. Could you speak slowly as much as possible. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So let's go back to the question. You've given evidence today that you returned fire on what you found to be military targets in areas where civilians lived; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I was very clear in my answer. We returned -- you say fire, but we returned fire in response to fire, and we opened fire on those areas from which fire was opened against us and killed our people, our women, our men, because there was no other way of stopping the killing. For instance, in the area where I was, in the Serbian Ilidza, unless you returned fire there was no other way. You could not just plead with someone, please don't open fire anymore. You killed 20 of my men today. So you had to reply. You had to respond to the fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: For I think the fourth time now: You responded to the fire which came from areas where civilians lived; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- specific --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- this is a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- you on the map --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure what the first word that the witness said was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My -- my definitive answer is we did not open fire on areas where there were civilians. We only opened fire and engaged targets from which fire was sowed against us. We never fired at areas where there were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mijatovic, at, I think, page 15 of today's evidence you talked about how you returned fire when Bosnian forces pulled out guns from underground parking lots in Alipasino Polje, and then at page 40, you said you agreed that Alipasino Polje had mainly high-rise buildings where civilians lived; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What did you return fire with, your mortars and artillery?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, more often than not mortars, small-calibre mortars, but it's very important to say at this point, Madam Prosecutor, that Alipasino Polje as a settlement in Sarajevo is a part where between buildings there are areas of over 200 metres of open space, and the Muslims would then use 155-millimetre howitzers, to place them there, and UNPROFOR warned them not to do that, because in that way they would risk being targeted, and I believe this is some seven -- this happened, for instance, in areas where there were 70 to 100 metres from --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- where the UNPROFOR was --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and also from between these buildings where --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's stick with the questions; all right? You said you returned fire with mortars. Would you agree with me that mortars are antipersonnel weapons?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, in principle.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, let's look at a number of the targets that you listed here. One of them is a police building. What kind of damage do you think a small-calibre mortar would do to a building?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a police station is a wartime military unit practically, because the armed forces consist of the military and --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You're not answering my question.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is very clear. What do you mean I'm not answer your question? If it is part of the enemy forces, if the police is part of the enemy forces, if it is taken out onto the front line, if they open fire if they themselves have mortars, for instance, that's very clear that that, too, would be a legitimate target, so the police building would be a legitimate military target --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's go back --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because it too is engaged in combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's go back to the question. I'm going to keep interrupting you so long as you don't answer the question, Mr. Mijatovic. Would you agree with me that a small-calibre mortar fired at a building is not going to do any significant damage?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I agree with you, but I don't know -- I don't understand the question. That's the problem. I'm saying I don't exclude that possibility. There were instances where we opened fire on the police station. I don't know why you're giving this particular example, but I assume that -- the assumption is that the police force is part of the armed forces, and in this case the police officers would come to the front line and open fire --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to intervene here. The witness said I can't recall that we opened fire, that we used 60-millimetre calibres to open fire on the police station, and I believe this is hypothetical. The witness is asked to guess. The witness said I can't recall that we opened fire from 60-millimetre weapons, and so how could he know what kind of damage would be incurred on the building?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The question was not whether police building was a legitimate target or not. Could you hear the -- listen to the question and answer -- answer it, please. Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So the question was whether you would agree with me that a small-calibre mortar fired at a building isn't going to do any significant damage.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President had a good remark. This is a hypothetical question, and, yes, it wouldn't cause a lot of damage. That is not at issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's find out --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not contestable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- whether VRS shelled or fired upon these targets listed in para 9 only in response or they fired shells on these. As far as these legitimate targets are concerned, they fired on its own initiative, and they fired only with mortars or something else. Then we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So is it your evidence, then, from your statement, Mr. Mijatovic, that your forces fired at the locations listed in paragraph 9?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown the statement in the Serbian language? If he don't have it, I have a copy here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: List those locations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've given evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we upload 1D8564. Yes, please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So it's your evidence that your forces shelled the police building, the Jusuf Dzonlic Barracks, the TAM spare parts warehouse, underground shelters in the area of Medjunarodnog Prijateljstva square near the PTT, the Gras garages near the geodesic institute, the wire factory --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not correct. Can we have a reference? Where is it that the witness said that they opened fire at this? This paragraph, paragraph 9, relates to the identification of targets, not areas where they opened fire at.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I just get to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, target maybe means they fired at it and then the Prosecution is fairly, legitimate to put such questions. It is for the witness to answer. So do you remember this map that you marked, Mr. Mijatovic? Do you see the marked map in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, but, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- it is not the same to open fire --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question was whether you see this map. So you see it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The question was -- from Ms. Edgerton was that whether you opened fire at these places.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The area, that's a wider term. When I -- or, rather, the Prosecutor, when she says garages, that could imply underground garages, 100 or 1.000 of them. Here, specifically, there's one garage in a very specific place where guns were deployed, 115 howitzer -- howitzers, and they opened fire from there at us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please, listen to the question. I asked you -- what Ms. Edgerton asked was whether you fired these marked places. You marked the places. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But only when fire was opened at us from those places. We didn't just open fire for no reason at all. Only when there was fire opened at us from those places we responded. That's specific. I can't be more specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you opened fire -- so when you fired on these places, you fired with -- your evidence is you fired with mortars and artillery, but usually small-calibre mortars; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I never even meant -- mentioned artillery, to be more specific. It could be that there were such instances, but my reply was that we only returned fire when fire was opened at us. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you fired -- I'll ask the question a second time. When you fired on these places, you fired -- your evidence is that you fired with mortars, possibly with artillery, but usually with small-calibre mortars; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The places shown, I can't even remember that artillery was used, but I cannot exclude it altogether. We did use mortars, and I have to repeat, we only returned fire when fire was opened at us. In other words, when there was fire opened from those places at us, we then returned fire with fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What calibre of mortars did you return the fire with?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can recall, we used the 60 and the 82 calibres.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So this -- this Chamber has actually heard evidence that mortars fired at the buildings in and around Sarajevo would have little to no effect because of the construction of the buildings and the size of the mortars, which were either for the most part around 82 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And for the record, Your Honours, that's General Fraser at T8009 to 8010.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So now knowing that, Mr. Mijatovic, I put it to you that at its very best, this kind of fire was only harassment fire.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was not, in the final analysis, our goal to cause losses among the enemy lines. It was really to harass them so that they would stop opening fire at us, so that they would stop sowing death on our side that we were defending.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you knew, because you've given evidence to this effect, that there were civilians in the area. You've said that the Alipasino Polje area was a civilian area; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You've agreed that mortars are antipersonnel weapons, so given that, given the risk of the spread of shrapnel when you use a mortar, and given that Alipasino Polje was a civilian area, you would actually expect that there was a significant risk, a high risk, that there would be civilian casualties from using mortars on those areas, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, because our observers who were observing and reporting to us where the fire was coming from, they were in a position to see that there were no civilians around the weapon that is firing shells at our side and killing people on the Serb Ilidza. So observers reported to us and said that within a diameter of about 200 metres everything was clear except for the weapon that was firing at our side. So that was always a way to avoid collateral damage that was referred to in previous trials. So that was a very effective way of protecting civilians --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and being sure and convinced of -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, before meeting Dr. Karadzic this week, you must have met with a representative of his Defence team to give the first draft of your statement, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just had this one meeting with the gentleman who is present here, Mr. Marko - he's a lawyer - Sladojevic. We just meant once and it was a relatively short meeting, I can say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you didn't tell him then that you had some military observers available to our brigade, did you? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did say that to Mr. Marko, and why it's not in the record, probably because time was so short, but I did say that. He's here, so let him say whether that is right or not right, because I even explained to him where the observers were at several locations, and I'm surprised that that didn't make it into that record or statement. Because we did --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam -- Madam Prosecutor, I beg your pardon. We did have our observers at several locations. That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And then after doing the first draft of your statement, you went out -- you met with Mr. Sladojevic again and you went out to the gaol and you met with Dr. Karadzic, and you didn't tell him about the observers then, did you? Because if you had, it would have been in your statement.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but you're not right. I did say then when I was with Mr. Karadzic, the President, I did say about these observers. Well, you see, many things can be said. I will just tell you a detail from my biography. I lived through clinical death myself. That is a major thing, Madam Prosecutor, and I even omitted to mention that, and that is something that is important for anyone. Do you understand that? Clinical death in --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in a war, in wartime. Let me just say this.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
