utterances.text: And you just talked, you just -- you just mentioned -- actually, if I could have your indulgence for a second.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise. May I just --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. Thank you. You just mentioned other trials in this Tribunal dealing -- you just mentioned other trials in this Tribunal on -- actually, I'll quote it to you. You said: "So reported to us," at page 50, line 12, "So reported to us and said within a diameter of 200 metres everything was clear except for the weapon that was firing on our side, so that was always a way to avoid collateral damage that was referred to in previous trials." What previous trials are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant specifically when I attended as a witness at

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Remember we talked about Poljanica before below Igman and we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We understood you and, if necessary, Mr. Karadzic will take that up that issue in his re-examination, but at this moment the question about a diameter of 200 metres and in what case. Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I'll put it to you, actually, Mr. Mijatovic, that the 200-metre diameter was actually not a consideration at all in --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Actually, I hesitate for a moment, Your Honour, and before I misspeak, can we go back and have a redaction of page 52, lines 8 and 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Witness, I put it to you that the diameter of 200 metres was a consideration not dealt with in any other trial in this Tribunal until the case against Generals Gotovina and Markac. That's the trial you were referring to, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had the feeling that it was mentioned in Mr. Galic's case and the case of other officers. That's my feeling. I mean, these 200 metres. But, well, I don't see what it is that is so important here, that you insist on that so much. Sorry about that. I don't understand. I mean, I don't know how to put it in a different way --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Then we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I really don't see what it is you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Then we'll move on. Let's go further down the list of military targets. In paragraphs 34 to 37 of your statement, you gave an additional list of targets following your interview with Dr. Karadzic at the gaol. Now, did you add this list of targets in those paragraphs because you fired on them?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have anything before me, so I cannot see what it is that you're speaking about now. I don't have anything on the screen, absolutely nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you say that you have a copy of your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In hard copy Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't have a copy of my statement, and I don't have anything on these screens, so I don't have a printed document, and I don't have it here, and I don't know what it is that is being said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When we have our usher back, you will have a hard copy of your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I can offer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's wait.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With your indulgence in the meanwhile for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So how about, Mr. Mijatovic, you turn over to page 6 of your statement and have a look at paragraphs 34 and onward. I want to know if you added those targets to your statement because you fired on them.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you please repeat the question, because I don't seem to understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you list all these places in paragraphs 34, 35, 36, 37 of your statement because your forces fired on them?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mentioned them because that's where they fired from against us. I'm not saying that we fired at them. I mention here from where we were attacked, from where our defence positions were attacked.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So did you mention these places because they were suggested to you during your meeting with Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not suggested to me. Rather, when I said during this conversation, when I spoke about all the casualties that the Ilidza Brigade had had, I don't know if you were following, but it was 460 men who were killed, which is a high percentage.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2.150 were wounded, many of them seriously wounded and therefore never returned to normal life or to the unit itself, and then if you look at what the enemy forces were, then I explained which forces these were, the 105th, the 101st, 102nd and 104th Brigade and they had all these weapons and my intention was obviously to indicate --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- allow me, please, Madam Prosecutor to indicate that -- which brigades these were the equivalent is 15- or 16.000 men against our --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- our 3.000 defenders who were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic, the question I asked you was did you mention these places because they were suggested to you and your answer was they weren't suggested to me. Can we leave it at that and move on? So your evidence is you didn't fire -- your forces didn't fire at any of these locations that you mention in paragraphs 34 to 37; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That is not correct. So you did fire at these locations.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The locations from where these brigades fired at us. So it was only firing positions and a firing position is a place from which a weapon fires at us. So it was only that weapon that we opened fire at, the weapon that fired at us. So that would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. So these locations that you list here are in, as I can see, areas that include Dobrinja, Aerodromsko Naselje, Hrasnica and Butmir. You would agree with me that these are all locations where civilians live, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilians did not live on the actual front line. It was only attackers who were there only, attackers from the enemy side, the enemy that was attacking us.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic, is Dobrinja a civilian area; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, yes, but civilians did not live at where the lines of combat were.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Aerodromsko Naselje is that a civilian area, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This should be clear to you. Partly it was militarised and partly it was civilian, and other settlements near the front line were of the same nature. Near the front line it was military and further afield it was civilian.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Hrasnica, was that a civilian area, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a large part, militaristic, military, and all of those parts that bordered Hrasnica and other civilian areas were military but then there were other areas that were civilian.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you when you returned fire on locations that fired on you in these areas, did you do that with your mortars and artillery?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most often it was small weapons that were involved in combat. There were also situations when at the lines of combat, I mean in these firing positions, too, because you know firing positions, whatever you wish to call them, but these firing positions from where fire was opened at us and we responded with fire. So we responded with fire to their fire, fire coming from their weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So is your answer that you responded with mortars and with artillery or not?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their artillery, their mortars, their fire coming from such weaponry we responded with corresponding weapons and pieces.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Similar question as before. Given the nature of mortars as antipersonnel weapons with a high risk of shrapnel spread from their impact, do you accept there would be a high risk of civilian casualties when you respond with fire in these areas we've been talking about?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not accept that, because we always took care of this, that observers should inform us whether there were civilians around there, and then we would fire at their mortars using our mortars or we would fire at their artillery using our artillery.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, let's try this then. So based on everything you've said up to now, let me put something to you. Is it your position that it would be inappropriate in Sarajevo to fire mortars or artillery at a military object in a civilian area without direct observation because you've talked about that and without confirmation that there were no civilians within a 200-metre radius?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could not rely on that as a rule if one is in a position where the enemy uses all available forces to attack our positions and our lines with the aim of taking over Ilidza and carry out a massacre by killing the population or driving it away. Or, for example, what was taking place? Our observers were killed by the enemy side, by their -- with their artillery, and we can see where the fire is coming from, and we know where it's coming from, Madam Prosecutor. Well, it would have been irresponsible not to return fire with fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I want to move on to another area now. You talked about air-bombs in your statement, and it seems like you know something about them, so I want to put the following propositions to you: First of all, do you agree with me that an air-bomb is a very powerful weapon with -- that carries a minimum of a hundred kilos of explosives?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In some cases even more, up to 250.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how it seems to you, because there were thousands of tasks in such situations in the war --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Mr. Mijatovic --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- so there were problems --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I don't know much about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That was a yes-or-no kind of question. Let's move on. So with hundred kilos -- a hundred kilos of explosives, do you agree with me that the potential destructive power of an air-bomb is sizable, massive, in fact?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, as Chief of Staff of the Ilidza Brigade in 1994 and 1995, you must have ordered the use of these weapons.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not order their use. There was subordination in place. There were people above me. I didn't. I claim that with full responsibility. I did not order that such weapons be used.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, if you know so much about them, you must have taken part in the testing of these weapons then, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You must have seen them firing?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion, yes. Sorry, if I may. If I may clarify something, whether I was engaged in testing. If that means practical testing, I did not take part in that. There were certain suggestions along at that line, but I was never engaged in the practical testing.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you weren't engaged in the testing. You only saw it being fired on one occasion. Did you ever see it hitting a target?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, twice. Three times. Once when we targeted a refrigeration facility; another time when it did not explode in Hrasnica. It landed where their mortars were and 120- and 82-millimetre weapons; and once when it fell where the tanks were in Ogrev. So thrice in total. We had five air-bombs. So these were three. Two were fired at the refrigeration facility and it landed just short of it, and the other two were used at Bjelasnica against the enemy side, in the forest, if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you said --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I was aware of five, and -- according to my knowledge, and I think it was a realistic assessment. There were five air-bombs in total, and three were used on Ilidza and two on Bjelasnica at the front line.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So let's have a look at P5943, which is a VRS Main Staff report to the president, dated 7 April 1995. And I'd like to go to page 5 of the English, paragraph 3(B) and B/C/S page 3, almost at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So it seems to me that you might have missed one, Mr. Mijatovic, because this document reports to the president that on this day the enemy activity was adequately responded to whereby a 250-kilo air-bomb was launched on the centre of Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, where do you find that?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On your copy, go down to paragraph 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Top --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Top of the page, 3B.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On his copy it would be almost at the bottom of the page, paragraph 3(B), just above paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the heading of (B) says: "Situation in the corps."

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it now. So it was adequately responded to enemy action. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's right. So it seems like there's an additional incident that you didn't know about.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Who fired it? It says on the centre of Hrasnica. The centre should be a very small part. The forward part where the lines were and the assets I mentioned. I don't have the centre in my version. Rather, a term is used which depicts extremely small areas in enemy front lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Maybe -- maybe --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's actually a cent, which is only 100th of a metre, meaning centimetre. If we go by that, that would be in the centre of Hrasnica, very close to the lines. That's the notion of centimetre.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Why don't you go over and have a look at paragraph 25 of your statement, Mr. Mijatovic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Incident G10, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is reading too fast interpreters note.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Mijatovic, are -- Mr. Mijatovic, you actually were well aware, according to your statement, of the incident in Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We weren't -- this says nothing about whether I was informed about the incident in Hrasnica. This only goes to my knowledge as to the deployment of enemy forces. If I know that the US sixth fleet is in the Adriatic, it doesn't mean that I know where they will engage tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, so in your statement, then, where you talk about the deployment of enemy forces in Hrasnica, are we to understand that, to your mind, a 250-kilo air-bomb was an appropriate weapon to use against 120-millimetre mortar nest?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not it. It wasn't one mortar as it was interpreted to me. When you have a mortar nest, there are several, two, three, up to five mortars within a 50-metre radius. A mortar nest always has more than one mortar.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. My question was whether we're to understand that, to your mind, a 250-kilo air-bomb was an appropriate weapon to use against 120-millimetre mortar nest. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not allowed to elicit the witness's opinion. Why should it be allowed to the Prosecution? Perhaps we should hear first what the witness knows rather than thinks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it's a totally inappropriate intervention at this time. Please answer the question, Mr. Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since obviously in a rush many things were omitted here, I don't see the tanks mentioned here, which were mentioned as part of the 104th Brigade, and that was in the area of Hrasnica. No one's talking about the 150- and 105-millimetre howitzers in Hrasnica. Rather, things were being suggested to me. The only thing you didn't ask me whether there was a pistol there which we targeted by using an air-bomb.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So still on the subject of air-bombs but in another vein, if you know something about them, you must know that they're powered by rocket fuel; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know approximately that it uses some kind of rocket fuel, but I'm not familiar with any details. What you said is the extent of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when the fuel runs out, the rocket -- the bomb drops. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So on what basis, then, can you, as you do in paragraph 18, knowing that talk about the proper function of air-bombs and the need for imprecision, possible errors and deviations to be reduced to a minimum? These weapons were actually inherently inaccurate, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was imprecise. Namely when I said that I didn't take part in the experimenting, it is a fact, though, and there was a witness in this courtroom whose testimony I followed. I learned again through stories that there were deviations, that, for example, a bomb sent one way would not exactly follow the trajectory, and I asked why and what happened, and then I was told that on occasion there would be a malfunctioning engine, and the remaining three engines would push it out of control. Then I requested that the -- a way be found or equipment created to take care of that or to carry out checks that all engines are properly functioning, and we -- there was a witness here who was in charge of establishing that procedure, to have a team of electronics engineers where engines were tested, and in such circumstances the bomb always travelled the desired route. So there was no longer any possibility that it would deviate you to a malfunctioning engine. I told you that the engines were controlled at first in the factory and then at the firing place itself where the engines were checked, and only then it could be known that it would travel the desired route and distance. One cannot --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] so --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- say on account of all that that it was imprecise.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So taking what you've just said, if we go back over to this incident G10 that you referred to in paragraph 25, taking what you just said and knowing that a civilian house in Hrasnica, this partly civilian community that you've described was demolished because of the impact of that air-bomb, are we meant to understand that you meant to target the civilian house?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No house was destroyed in that area. It's an enemy lie. Our observers told us about the unexploded one, whereas the other one exploded on Ogrev. At Ogrev there were no houses in the vicinity. It's an enemy line. I even had an opportunity to see their report if that's what you had in mind. It was drafted two years after the war and one can see it's a lie because, Madam Prosecutor, they said that five air-bombs were launched at Hrasnica. It's a lie. There were only two. So they start lying with the numbers and places where those bombs fell.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think we'll move on to another area, and it relates to something that you referred to in the paragraphs of your statement that you added after having seen Dr. Karadzic. In those additions you offered us a number of documents that you say describe your relationship with UNPROFOR, and you say that the brigade didn't cause problems with them except when they abused their mandate, but on reading that, I recalled in March 1995, the SRK closed all the land routes into Sarajevo including those in the area of the Ilidza Brigade. Didn't that cause problems with UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In March 1995? Well, if so, to be honest, I can't really recall it as I sit here, but there must have been very good reasons for something like that. And I was not responsible for the area of responsibility of the corps. I was only responsible for my own zone, and that's -- my command would have been responsible for that, too, and there must have been very strong reasons if that's what happened --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that's what was done. I'm trying to recall where I was in March 1995, and that's not easy. You have to admit that. I mean, you should have put this question to someone from the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot really speak for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In July 1995, the problems actually got a little bit more serious, and maybe we'll have a document, P897, called up to have a look at that. In July 1995, your forces shelled UN convoys who were bringing aid into the city over Mount Igman, and I don't think there's a translation of this -- oh, there is. What a surprise. In that case, we'll go to English page 4. This document is an UNPROFOR weekly sitrep dated 15 July 1995 and refers to an attack on the Igman road that devastates an aid convoy, and if we -- and --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My apologies. I didn't realise, Your Honours, that a B/C/S translation is available, but I would be grateful to my friends if they would find the relevant paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I think we are there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It reports in the paragraph that's headed: "Attacks on the Igman road, aid convoy devastated, French retaliate," which is at the -- if you could scroll down on the B/C/S page. That's the heading. And then the text, relevant text, would be over on the next page of the English. This report reads that: "On Friday evening, 14 July, an UNPROFOR UNHCR convoy of four vehicles carrying flour over Igman was attacked from Serb-held flats below the mountain. "A 30-millimetre cannon and a 76-millimetre tank weapon fired from Bacevo and a T-55 fired from Gornji Kotorac. Two of the four vehicles were destroyed on another was damaged." Now, this doesn't appear to be an example of UNPROFOR exceeding their mandate at all and yet they were fired upon.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is there a question for me? Well, first of all, and I'm not sure that the translation is good, and I hope that people who can speak both Serbian and English follow this, we didn't have a 30-millimetre cannon, nor do I know that there was a T-76-millimetre tank used during this work. So immediately judging from that you can see that this report is not accurate. We neither had this cannon nor a 76-millimetre tank. So this now puts into question your entire claim here and question. We did not have this cannon, and I say with -- this with full responsibility. Nor did we have a 76-millimetre tank. That's what I'm reading here. So we were not the ones who opened fire, because -- that's obvious, because we did not have these assets.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or -- or -- just look at this, please. Please allow me. Serbs returned fire with 78-millimetre calibre shells. That, too, does not exist. So all these assets, all these weapons mentioned here, they're just a fabrication. There is no 78-millimetre weapon, nor do I know of any cannon, a 30-millimetre cannon, nor a 76-millimetre tank. There really were no such weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So somebody just sat down and wrote this off the top of their head.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, let's have a look at P1782, a SRK daily combat report to the VRS Main Staff for the 14 July -- 14th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The number again, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd better check with Mr. Reid, but -- apologies for a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: P1782 and I misspoke in terms of the date. 7 April 1995. That's the correct document. And let's go over in English to page 3. And in B/C/S, we also need paragraph 3. I'm not sure of the page number. In B/C/S you have to go over one further page. Thank you. Oh, no. Apologies. It's paragraph 3. It's displayed halfway through the page on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this is dated April 7, 1995, and it says: "Problems with UNPROFOR emerged in the Ilidza Infantry Brigade zone yesterday around 9.15 when UNPROFOR fired at our positions in the area of the forestry school, following our shooting at the Hrasnica-Igman road. After that, they came closer to the position of our Browning." And then further it says: "...today at around 7.30 in the morning, a UN unit positioned 4 APCs near our check-points in Nedzarici and later on 2 tanks as well, hindering normal contact between Nedzarici and the ... airport ...," and then, "the brigade blocked UNPROFOR." So UNPROFOR was again shot at on the Hrasnica-Igman road this time three months earlier than the first incident, by SRK forces. Are you disputing the accuracy of this report?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can neither dispute it nor confirm it, Madam Prosecutor. All I know is for your information and for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, that we worked well together with UNPROFOR. We co-operated. But there were also differences such as these, if I may call them that, because, and I've already explained this to the Defence and Mr. President, Mr. Karadzic, the -- namely the UNPROFOR was made up of members of the Foreign Legion, and these legionnaires, of course some of them were honourable but most of them just wanted to profit from other people's suffering and to profit from other people's suffering when you have an occasion is as follows: We saw -- --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- on the screens --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A numbers of times, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And of course you've met with Dragomir Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, also a number of times, and they're both honourable men.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you would have met them then both at the brigade command but also at corps headquarters at Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is no corps Main Staff. There's only one Main Staff. I want to make sure that there is no confusion here. There was a command of the main corps of -- there was a corps command, so we met as subordinate and superior at the corps command and the brigade command. So this would be the correct answer. There was only one Main Staff and that was --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- above the entire army.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, did General Galic and General Milosevic come to your brigade's area of responsibility to inspect the troops?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And how often would these inspections take place?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they could say they were regular, because after all it was part of their duties. So you could say that was on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would they visit the lines?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, and there were occasions where I went with them to visit the lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And would you describe them as very familiar with the situation in their corps overall?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well acquainted.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just one last question, just because you seem to have a friendly relationship with the President and you waved at him when you left the courtroom yesterday. How long have you known Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from before the war, but we didn't -- I didn't know him personally. We met during the war, or in fact from the time when the Serbian Democratic Party was established. That's for how long I've known of him. I've known of him from the press, the television, and so on. He was an admired person by the Serbian people. Is an admired person by the Serbian people. And had it not been for him, the Serbian people would not have remained on this side of the river, nor would it have survived in that area, because we saw in Kosovo and Macedonia and Slovenia and Croatia what was in store for Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you say "this side of the river," what river are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean the Drina River. The enemy's objective, and this was mentioned on numerous occasions in the media and on the TV in Slovenia and Croatia, and even to this day in Bosnia and Herzegovina Sefer Halilovic said that if need be, they would resolve the Serbian issue summarily and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last portion of his answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the last portion of your answer after resolving "the Serbian issue."

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to them, the enemy, that's what it meant. And I also added, but you had taken your headphones off so you couldn't have heard this, you probably didn't hear of the statement by the commander of the so-called Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, General Halilovic's. It again introduced a certain level of friction in that area and caused unrest, because he openly on TV and through the media again issued threats to Serbs, saying that he would handle us summarily or take care of us summarily, us Serbs, and he's just one of many of those who keep issuing threats and using warmongering --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- speeches.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the same is true of Izetbegovic and -- --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Bakir Izetbegovic and --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. You did much more than repeat the last portion of your answer. I'm over time, Your Honours, so I'm concluding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You didn't deal with the video-clip at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Recognising that I'm over time, Your Honours, I chose to not deal with it and focus on other areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination? How long would you need?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Between 15 to 20 minutes and perhaps even less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we have a break -- a short break?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, can we try to do it without the break, because that will make it faster. If I elicit short answers we can go on without a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Then let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major sir, it was suggested to you that you met with me at the Detention Unit. Did you meet with me in the Detention Unit, and how did we have your statement confirmed?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my great regret, Mr. President, we did not meet directly. We spoke via link that was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end. Could all other microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters said they couldn't hear the last part of the witness's answer. What did you say? "We spoke via link," and then? What did you say after you mentioned videolink -- via link?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said it was to my great regret that we did not talk directly that we talked through this videolink. That is what I said. That's all I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did I suggest those positions to you and those locations where the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was, or how was it that I asked you about the forces that were facing you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, and I'm responding to Their Honours, you could not suggest that to me. If anyone could have suggested anything to anyone, only I could have suggested this to you, because I'm from the area. I spent the war there. There was no need for any kind of suggestion coming from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There was the question of your information about the existence of observers in your brigade and that that was not reflected in your statement. Do you know of any brigades that did not have observers?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that nowhere in the world is there a brigade that did not have one, let alone the Army of Republika Srpska. They were certainly one of the most disciplined armies in the world. There is simply no brigade anywhere without observers; not only in our area but anywhere in the world, any army anywhere in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In line 50 today there was mention of whether civilians were present at firing positions. Let me ask you this: Did you allow the following: While artillery pieces were firing, could civilians gather around that artillery piece?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way. That is a basic rule of warfare anywhere that civilians should not be close to weapons that are firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking, for instance, whether the Muslim side assembled civilians while they were firing at you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. That is impossible for any normal person to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 49, Witness Fraser was mentioned, and it was noted that he said that with your mortars you could not damage buildings at all. What was your objective? Was your objective to destroy buildings in Alipasino Polje? What could you use to destroy buildings there?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, this was never our intention or our objective to fire at civilian facilities or civilians, not only in Alipasino Polje but anywhere in Republika Srpska. I state that with full responsibility. Wherever I was at any front line, that was never the objective and that was never the intention to fire at civilians and civilian facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If it would be your objective to destroy buildings, massive strong buildings, what could you use to break down such buildings, what kind of weaponry?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we'd have to use heavy calibres to damage a building. These are howitzers or cannons or tanks. Those are weapons for destroying buildings, but I repeat once again it was not our objective or our intention to do that. On the contrary, although we ourselves knew of the law of war and the Geneva Conventions, we did receive orders that were of a permanent nature, a lasting nature, not to fire, not even to use the weapons that we did have, nothing against civilians or civilian facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have in e-court D331.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is an intercept, a conversation between myself and the late Danilo Veselinovic. Did you know who Danilo Veselinovic was?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him personally, Mr. President, but I don't have that here now -- oh, just a moment. Yes, I have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is the 13th of April, 1992. Can we have page 2 both in English and in Serbian. It was suggested to you that I knew about fire against Hrasnica and it was implied that I accepted civilian casualties. Please let us look at line 8 or 9 from up here: "Radovan Karadzic: Aha, to probably the traffic-light the sports hall. And then Veselinovic says: "Yes, the hall." "Which sports hall?" And then he says, Veselinovic: "At Mojmilo. Well, it's in our hands. Shall we blow it up or not?" And then further down I'm asking whether there are people there. And now can we have page 3 in Serbian in English we can keep this one. It's towards the bottom of the page in English here. And Danilo is saying: "Should I fire?" And I say: "Yes, it is important that there are no people there, that there won't be any civilian casualties." Does this correspond to your knowledge about our attitude towards Muslim civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, when Serbs say "bignoti [phoen]," that means "to take" or, rather, to -- to -- but then, you know, in the jargon also I don't know whether the people who are present here -- when this verb is used, say, in Sarajevo, that would mean that somebody stole my wallet, my coat or something like that. So that verb was used like meaning to steal, to nick, if you will. I know that you were very explicit, very imperative. You always said that fire should not be opened. You and also the Main Staff headed by General Mladic and also the corps commands and the brigade commands said that civilians and civilian facilities should not be fired at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But on this page here in Serbian it says "should we fire?" So that is where there was a warehouse of looted goods. And he says, "should I fire?" And then my answer is that it is important that there are no people there. But, thank you, you've answered my question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please have 1D3002. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we please take a look at this. This is the 16th of February, 1994. This is a meeting with Galic, an UNPROFOR meeting, a meeting of the UNPROFOR commander with him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have a translation here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read it out in English and then you will receive interpretation.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just five. [In English] "Regrouping of Bosnia of weapons": "As they are very concerned with the area south-east of Sarajevo, I told them that I will ask the Bosnian side to regroup heavy weapons from Butmir, Sokolovic and Hrasnica in one location under UNPROFOR control." [Interpretation] Before I put my question, let me just remind you this is the 16th of February, 1994, and there was this promise given to General Galic as to what UNPROFOR will do with Muslims weapons to the south-west of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please look at 1D8374. 1D8374.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this. You have it in Serbian. There's a reference to the 14th of July, and could you please take a look at this here. It says that we started an artillery attack on an unannounced convoy of trucks travelling along the so-called Igman road. Do you remember that it was the duty of UNPROFOR to announce their convoys including the vehicles and goods involved?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that very well. That was the obligation of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I shall rephrase. Major, why did it say unannounced convoy here?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is quite clear to me. There was no need for this reaction on the part of Madam Prosecutor. I am one of the persons who carried out the measures agreed between UNPROFOR and the Serb side, and there were no problems whenever they were announced and when they were not smuggling ammunition and weapons into Sarajevo. So one just had to have this goodwill and announce the convoy and then there would be no problems whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did their mandate include escorting trucks of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That did not -- that was not part of their mandate. On the contrary, that was a violation of the agreements with the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm now going to read out this other paragraph: Our artillery fire was counteracted by mortar shells and machine-gun fire from the enemy position on Igman, Hrasnica and Sokolovic Kolonija as well as the firing positions and assets of UNPROFOR. That obligation from February 1994 that they will regroup and remove these weapons from these Muslim settlements, was that honoured?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew. Our observers reported to us directly and regularly and we knew that this had not been honoured and that is true because on the 14th of July there were already rapid deployment forces stationed at UNPROFOR together with UNPROFOR. And now why do I remember this? On the 14th of July the parents of my military policeman got killed within the hospital compound. So it was the hospital that was shelled on that day from all directions, not only Sokolovic Kolonija but Butmir but also from Igman where these rapid deployment forces were and where UNPROFOR was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you just one more document, 1D6451, please. Can these two that we've already seen be admitted, Excellency?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether you asked anything about the previous document. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I was just pointing out this document 1D03002 is actually already admitted as P02120. That's the previous document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And you have no objection to admit the last document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will admit it as next Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 1D8374 receives number D2512, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Along with an apology for not having this translated yet, I mean this document, but indeed the need cropped up for that. I'll read it out: "On the basis of daily reports of duty officers of battalions, we hereby notify you that during the last night and day the enemy did not abide by the signed cease-fire because constant provocations went on by sniper fire from the directions of Oslobodjenje, Dobrinja 5, Butmir. We did not respond to fire. We did not have any casualties, any wounded or dead." What was the usual thing? When did you not respond with fire?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We have a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And what is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this reflect the truth, that fire was opened from these positions, that the Serb side did not respond unless they had any casualties, wounded or dead?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, sometimes it happened that we had both dead and wounded and did not respond nevertheless. Why? Believe me, I conducted an analysis. Most of our dead lost their lives during cease-fires, because the Serbs fully observed the cease-fire whereas the enemy side, the Muslims, did not and this is correct what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could I ask you now that you read paragraph 3 while we're waiting for the translation, that is the situation in the area of responsibility of our brigade and then?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. UNPROFOR is carrying out its regular tasks and today it was observed that it was escorting a column of Turkish trucks up Igman. The reference is to Muslim forces, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were they allowed to do that according to their mandate?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was obvious. I think that once or twice I said that. I said that. Sometimes they were fair in their co-operation and sometimes they were unfair. When I say unfair, I'm saying this: This is abuse of their mission. I mean, the mission of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Major. I have no further questions. Can this document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D6451 receives number D2513, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As regards the three video-clips you used in your examination-in-chief, Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber finds the first one, i.e., 1D6482, not relevant to this case. However, as regards the remainder of those three, i.e., 1D6483 and 1D6484, albeit marginally, the Chamber finds it relevant so that we'll admit those two. Shall we give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D6483 receives number D2514, Your Honours, and document 1D6484 receives number D2515, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first two that were untranslated were even more important for the Defence, but in order not to have to keep the witness here, by your leave, we will seek to tender them through his commander or someone else from his brigade who could testify to the contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you are not going to keep the witness until next week. Very well. Then that concludes your evidence, Mr. Mijatovic. I thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go. But we will rise altogether -- yes. You may be excused Mr. Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for having listened to me patiently, and as for you, Mr. President, I hope you get out as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In light of the time, I'll try to be very brief. We've had a lot of scheduling changes which we've tried to accommodate, although with considerable strain to our resources and personnel during the process. Now we have another change for next week. A witness has been accelerated. Again, we're going to try to accommodate that as we've indicated to Mr. Robinson. That witness is currently scheduled for the last day of the week on Thursday. The position agreed upon by the parties has been that he would be fixed for that date even though there is some concern about the -- whether or not the number of available witnesses will consume the entire portion of the week. So even if -- if we finish with the other witnesses earlier, that witness would still be heard on Thursday, and I just wanted to confirm that with the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see no problem there. So we'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. We'll be sitting in the afternoon on Monday next week. The hearing is now adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 3rd day of December, 2012, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.57 p.m.,
